subject: PSHE
source: National Curriculum / statutory RSHE guidance (Relationships Education, Relationships and Sex Education, Health Education); PSHE Association programme of study themes and KS3 mental health lessons (Drive PSHE folder); TGA RSHE Policy 2026-27, Careers Education and Guidance Policy and RECIPE Character Framework 2026-27 (Drive); existing TGA PSHE Y5 lesson style. Qur'an and hadith references limited to well-known authenticated sources and cited plainly. RSE is taught from an Islamic perspective, to boys and girls separately; parents can see all RSE materials.

lessons.title: Bullying, prejudice and being an upstander
objectives: Explain the forms and effects of bullying, including cyberbullying and discrimination
Describe how the Equality Act 2010 protects people from discrimination
Plan safe, effective ways to challenge prejudice and support others

keywords.def: treating someone unfairly because of who they are
an unfair opinion formed without knowing someone
a feature of a person protected by equality law
bullying through phones, apps or online games
a person who safely supports someone being mistreated

starter: Bismillah. Define bullying in your own words.
Name one way an upstander can help.

teach.heading: Types and effects of bullying
bullets: Physical, verbal, social and online
Targets someone repeatedly and on purpose
Can harm confidence, sleep and learning
Never the victim's fault
teach.note: Say bismillah. Revise the definition: deliberate, repeated, hurtful, with an imbalance of power. Discuss forms including exclusion, spreading rumours, impersonation and sharing humiliating content. Explain that effects can last, and that bullying is a serious matter under the TGA Anti-Bullying and Cyberbullying Policy. Do not ask for personal experiences. Link to RECIPE Integrity. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Prejudice and discrimination
bullets: Prejudice is an unfair opinion
Discrimination is unfair treatment
Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics
Includes race, religion, sex, disability and age
teach.note: List the protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation. Explain that the Act is the law in Great Britain. Pupils may have experienced prejudice, including Islamophobia, so create a safe space and allow pupils to pass. Teach that prejudice affects how people are treated, and that it is wrong. Ask: ‘How do stereotypes begin?’

teach.heading: What Islam teaches
bullets: Qur'an 49:13: we were made into peoples to know each other
The most honoured is the most mindful of Allah
Qur'an 49:11: do not mock or insult
Hadith: do not harm or return harm
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 49:13 says that Allah created people into nations and tribes so that they may know one another, and the most honoured is the most mindful of Allah. Cite Qur'an 49:11 on mocking. Also cite the hadith ‘There should be neither harming nor reciprocating harm’ (Ibn Majah and Ahmad; Nawawi's Forty Hadith no. 32). Discuss how these teachings apply to our behaviour towards everyone, regardless of background.

teach.heading: Challenging unkindness safely
bullets: Do not join in or share
Support the person privately
Calmly say: ‘That is not okay.’
Report to a trusted adult or DSL
teach.note: Teach the ‘4 Ds’ in simple form: distract, delegate (tell an adult), delay (check in later), direct (speak up if it is safe). Emphasise that safety comes first. Practise: ‘That joke is not funny.’ Discuss why bystanders often do nothing and how one voice can change a group. Link to RECIPE Integrity and Excellence.

teach.heading: The law and reporting
bullets: Some online behaviour can be a crime
Threats, harassment and hate crime are serious
Keep evidence: screenshots, dates
Report: TGA staff, platform, police, Childline
teach.note: Explain that sending threatening or grossly offensive messages can be a criminal offence, and that hate crime is taken seriously. Remind pupils to save evidence rather than reply. Show how to report within an app. Emphasise that pupils will be supported and listened to. Remind them of Childline (0800 1111) and the TGA reporting routes.

practice: Match the protected characteristic: (a) being treated unfairly because of a hijab (b) being mocked for needing a wheelchair (c) being excluded because of age.
Write a response a pupil could use if someone makes a hurtful joke about another pupil's background.
Is it bullying? Explain: ‘Bilal is left out of the group chat every day and the others post jokes about him.’
independent: Write a short case study of an upstander making a safe choice, with three steps taken.
Create an anti-bullying pledge for the class that includes one reference to Qur'an 49:11 or 49:13.
Explain in a paragraph the difference between prejudice and discrimination, with examples.
exit: Name two protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.
Give one safe action an upstander can take.
lessons.homework: Interview a trusted adult about how they handled unkindness at school or work, and write four sentences about their advice.
lessons.send: SEND: provide scenario cards with sentence starters for responses. EAL: pre-teach key terms with examples. Stretch: research one historical example of a person who challenged discrimination and present how they did it.

lessons.title: Peer influence and risky substances: vaping, alcohol and drugs
objectives: Explain how peer influence and social norms affect decisions about substances
Describe the health, legal and Islamic perspectives on vaping, alcohol and drugs
Use assertive strategies and know where to get help

keywords.def: being unable to stop using something even when it harms you
an addictive drug in cigarettes and many vapes
what most people actually do or think is normal
a substance that affects the mind, such as alcohol
the intellect or reason

starter: Bismillah. Name two assertive phrases for saying no.
Why is it important to protect our health?

teach.heading: Does everyone do it?
bullets: Most young people do not vape or drink
Perceived norms can be wrong
Influence comes from friends, media and social feeds
Choose the influences you follow
teach.note: Say bismillah. Begin with a poll question: ‘What percentage of young people your age do you think vape?’ Then explain that surveys consistently show a minority do, and that people overestimate what others do. Teach that the idea of ‘everyone does it’ is a pressure tactic. Link to RECIPE Integrity. This lesson is factual and non-judgemental: never ask pupils about their own or their family's behaviour. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Vaping and tobacco
bullets: Most vapes contain nicotine, which is addictive
Can affect concentration, mood and lungs
Illegal to sell to under 18s in the UK
Vapes are not harmless for young people
teach.note: Explain that vapes may help some adult smokers to quit but are not safe for children. Nicotine can lead to dependence and cravings, which can affect mood and concentration. Mention that long-term effects are still being studied. Do not exaggerate; use accurate facts. Link to the hadith that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said do not harm yourself or others (Ibn Majah and Ahmad). Misconception: vapes are just water vapour.

teach.heading: Alcohol and drugs
bullets: Alcohol affects judgement and safety
Illegal drugs such as cannabis carry risk and legal penalties
Drugs are classed A, B or C by law
Addiction can start after only a few uses
teach.note: Give accurate, age-appropriate facts: alcohol slows the brain and reduces judgement; illegal drugs are classified by the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971; cannabis is Class B; possession can lead to a criminal record. Teach that some medicines are drugs too and should be used only as directed. Do not give detail about how to use or obtain substances. Take questions through the question box.

teach.heading: The Islamic perspective
bullets: Qur'an 5:90: intoxicants are an abomination
Hadith: every intoxicant is khamr and haram
Protect the mind (aql) and the body
Choose good company and avoid harm
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 5:90 states that intoxicants and gambling are abominations of Satan's handiwork and should be avoided. Cite the hadith: every intoxicant is khamr and every khamr is forbidden (Muslim). Explain that protecting the intellect is among the aims of Islamic law. Discuss that Islam encourages leaving what harms us. Link to RECIPE Eeman and Integrity.

teach.heading: Saying no and getting help
bullets: Say no clearly and walk away
Suggest another activity
Leave and tell a trusted adult
teach.note: Practise three refusal styles: direct, with humour, with an excuse. Role-play in breakout rooms with an invented scenario of a friend offering a vape at a park. Remind pupils that they can contact FRANK (confidential drug advice) and Childline. Emphasise that asking for help for a friend is a caring act. If a pupil appears to be at risk, follow safeguarding procedures.

practice: True or false? (a) Most young people vape. (b) Nicotine is addictive. (c) It is legal for shops to sell vapes to under 18s.
Write two assertive responses to: ‘Just try it, everyone does.’
Explain in two sentences why protecting the mind is important in Islam.
independent: Create a fact sheet: ‘Seven facts about vaping and young people’.
Write a short script showing a pupil refusing a vape and suggesting something else.
Write a paragraph linking Qur'an 5:90 and the idea of aql to healthy choices.
exit: Give one assertive way to say no.
lessons.homework: Research the NHS or FRANK website on vaping and write three facts you learned and one question.
lessons.send: SEND: provide response cards and visuals for facts. EAL: pre-teach key words with images. Stretch: analyse an advert or social media post that glamorises substances and identify persuasion techniques.

lessons.title: Mental health: when feelings become too much
objectives: Recognise circumstances that can lead to intense emotions
Explain a range of healthy strategies and why some strategies are unhelpful
Assess whom, how and why to ask for support

keywords.def: persistent worry that is hard to control
feeling sad or flat for a long time
something that sets off a strong emotion
the people and services who can help you
trusting Allah after doing your best

starter: Name two people you could talk to when stressed.

teach.heading: When feelings become intense
bullets: Big events: exams, loss, conflict, change
Hormones and growing up affect mood
Feeling low or anxious sometimes is normal
Seek help if it lasts or stops daily life
teach.note: Say bismillah. Teach that everyone faces times of intense emotion: moving, a falling-out, exams, grief, illness. This lesson draws on the PSHE Association KS3 lesson ‘Healthy coping strategies’. Read the PSHE Association guidance ‘Preparing to teach about mental health’ before teaching. Do not ask for personal stories; use invented case studies. Keep language careful and avoid any detail of self-harm methods. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Unhelpful and helpful strategies
bullets: Unhelpful: bottling up, isolating, endless scrolling
Unhelpful: unkindness to others or risky habits
Helpful: talking, sleep, exercise, nature, creativity
Helpful: prayer, dhikr, du'a, Qur'an
teach.note: Use the invented case of Maryam, who stops replying to friends and stays up late scrolling after a bad test result. Ask: ‘Why might she do this? What are the short-term and long-term effects?’ Explain that unhelpful strategies may bring short-term relief but make things worse later. Pupils should identify a better plan for Maryam. Stress that if a strategy involves harming oneself, the right step is to tell a trusted adult.

teach.heading: Signs that someone needs support
bullets: Changes in sleep, appetite or energy
Withdrawing from friends and activities
Feeling hopeless or very anxious for weeks
Feeling unsafe or thinking of self-harm: tell someone today
teach.note: Teach pupils to notice changes in themselves and in friends. Keep this factual and calm. Explain that physical symptoms can also be signs of worry. Stress that no one should have to cope alone and that a friend who is struggling needs an adult, not just a secret. Provide the line: ‘I am worried about you and I'm going to tell someone who can help because I care.’

teach.heading: Islamic perspectives on hardship and help
bullets: Qur'an 2:286: Allah does not burden beyond capacity
Qur'an 94:5-6: with hardship comes ease
Hadith: every disease has a cure
Seeking help is part of tawakkul
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 2:286 and 94:5-6. Cite the hadith that Allah has not sent down a disease without sending down its cure (Bukhari). Explain that faith practices bring comfort and are part of a healthy routine, and that they go alongside talking to people and professional support when needed. Misconception: struggling means weak faith. Prophets experienced grief and hardship. Link to RECIPE Resilience.

teach.heading: Building your support network
bullets: Family and trusted adults
TGA pastoral team and DSL
GP and NHS 111
Childline 0800 1111; Shout: text 85258
teach.note: Ask pupils to draw their personal support network without sharing names. Show how to reach Childline and Shout (text 85258, free 24/7). Practise a sentence to start a conversation. Explain that in an emergency or if someone is in immediate danger they should call 999. Remind pupils to follow up and tell another adult if the first does not help.

practice: Sort into helpful or unhelpful: (a) going for a walk (b) staying up all night scrolling (c) talking to a trusted adult (d) ignoring friends for weeks.
Write what you would say to a friend who has been withdrawn and tired for a month.
Name three people or services you can contact for support.
independent: Write a plan for Maryam with three helpful steps and the people who can support her.
Create a leaflet: ‘Looking after your mind’ with five strategies and two helplines.
Write a paragraph explaining how faith and seeking help work together.
exit: Give one helpful and one unhelpful way to cope.
Where can you get free, confidential support?
lessons.homework: Write three self-care activities you can do this week and which trusted adult you would talk to if worried.
lessons.send: SEND: use a visual traffic-light strategy sort and allow breaks. EAL: provide vocabulary for emotions. Stretch: evaluate three mental health websites for reliability.

lessons.title: Body image, media and self-worth
objectives: Explain how filters, advertising and social media can distort body image
Develop strategies for healthy self-esteem and critical media literacy
Link contentment and gratitude to self-worth

keywords.def: how you think and feel about your body
a tool that alters how a photo or video looks
a person who is paid to promote products online
how you value yourself
contentment with what Allah has given

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between fact and opinion?
Name one way adverts persuade people.

teach.heading: What is body image?
bullets: How we see and feel about our bodies
Affected by family, friends and media
Boys and girls can both feel pressure
Can change over time
teach.note: Say bismillah. Define body image. Emphasise that many young people feel unsure about their appearance, and this is common. Discuss the pressure on boys (muscle, height) as well as girls. Do not use images of real people. Do not ask pupils to share their feelings about their bodies. Link to RECIPE Contentment. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: What you see is not always real
bullets: Filters, editing and lighting change images
Influencers are paid to sell products
Highlights are not everyday life
Ask: who gains if I feel unhappy?
teach.note: Show examples of edited images from stock or cartoon sources rather than real people. Explain that filters can change shape, skin and size. Ask pupils how they could check if an image is edited. Teach critical questions: Who made this? What do they want me to buy or believe? What is left out? Misconception: if lots of people look like that online, it must be normal.

teach.heading: Comparison and its effects
bullets: Constant comparison can lower mood
Unrealistic ideals can affect eating and exercise
Extreme diets and supplements can harm
Talk to a trusted adult or GP if worried
teach.note: Explain that comparing ourselves to edited images can make us feel worse. Mention that health professionals advise young people not to diet; they need a balanced intake to grow. Avoid details about eating disorders; simply state that worrying about food or weight that begins to take over is a reason to speak to a trusted adult or GP. Mention muscle-building supplements marketed to teenagers are not recommended.

teach.heading: Islamic teaching on worth and gratitude
bullets: Qur'an 95:4: created in the best of forms
Hadith: Allah looks at hearts and deeds
Shukr: be grateful for what you have
Real worth is character and taqwa
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 95:4 says that Allah created the human being in the best stature. Cite the hadith: Allah does not look at your appearance or wealth but at your hearts and deeds (Muslim). Link with Qur'an 49:13 on honour being linked to taqwa. Ask: ‘How is a person's worth measured?’ Link to RECIPE Contentment (shukr).

teach.heading: Building healthy self-esteem
bullets: Focus on what your body can do
Limit time with accounts that make you feel bad
Practise kind self-talk
Spend time on strengths, faith and service
teach.note: Teach pupils to unfollow or mute accounts that harm their mood. Practise reframing: ‘I look wrong’ becomes ‘My body helps me pray, learn and play.’ Encourage gratitude lists and acts of service as boosts to self-worth. Remind pupils that the pastoral team is available for private chats. Close with a short du'a of thanks.

practice: Spot the clues that an image has been edited. Write three questions you could ask about it.
Rewrite this self-talk: ‘I will never look as good as him.’
True or false? (a) Everyone online looks the way they do in their posts. (b) Influencers are often paid. (c) Worth depends on appearance in Islam.
independent: Create a ‘Media detective’ checklist with five questions to ask about any image or advert.
Write a note to a younger pupil about being content and confident.
Write a paragraph explaining how Qur'an 95:4 and the hadith about hearts and deeds support healthy self-worth.
exit: Name two ways that images can be unrealistic.
Give one habit that builds healthy self-esteem.
lessons.homework: List three things your body helps you do and three things you are grateful for. Share one with a family member.
lessons.send: SEND: use cartoon or object examples for editing and visual prompt cards. EAL: pre-teach vocabulary with images. Stretch: research how advertisers use persuasion techniques and evaluate one advert.
